To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we describe a new approach for promoter/TSS identification in trans-spliced genes and apply it to the Ciona intestinalistroponin I gene.
we developed and validated a method for mapping the promoters/transcription start sites for SL trans-spliced tunicate genes.

the promoter and transcription start site (TSS) for an SL trans- spliced gene can be mapped by two different experimental methods, both of which give the same result, namely that the TSS lies ∼460 bp upstream of the trans- splice acceptor site.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular mechanisms underlying transcriptional control of gene expression in eukaryotic cells.
the identification of the transcription start sites (and hence promoters) of genes that are trans-spliced.
the identification and characterization of cis-regulatory elements in SL trans-splicing genes, and we have developed two new methods that can be applied to the analysis of such genes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the two methods described here are both valid for mapping TSSs for trans spliced genes.

the two methods are both valid and reliable, but that the deletion method is more robust and more efficient, while the high-throughput 5′-cDNA sequencing method has the advantage of being able to detect and map minor TSSs.

the troponin I promoter in Ciona intestinalis has a single major TSS located ∣460 nt upstream from the 5′-most trans-splice accepter site and that this TSS is flanked by a TATA box 31 nt 3′ to the TSS.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the two methods described are broadly applicable to promoter mapping in SL trans- spliced genes, but that the deletion method is likely to be the most practical for routine use.
the troponin I promoter is located 460 nt upstream from the trans-splice site.
we developed and tested two methods for mapping TSSs in trans-spliced genes.
The main takeaway from our work is that
SL trans-splicing can occur at a distance of at least 460 nt from the acceptor site, and that SL trans-spliced pre-mRNA can be efficiently trans-spliced even in the absence of a TATA element.
it is possible to identify promoters/TSSs in trans-spliced genes by using a combination of experimental deletion of trans-acceptor sites and high-throughput sequencing of mRNA populations.
the two methods generate precise agreement for a trans-spliced gene in a tunicate, and that the two methods should be useful for promoter/TSS mapping in trans-spliced genes of other organisms.
